content: The national research priorities for leprosy should be developed collaboratively with all stakeholders in the national research network. These priorities must strike a balance between different types and broad topics of research. They should be treated as a living document, updated periodically, and integrated into national, regional, and global research plans. While the efficacy of rifampicin for contacts of leprosy patients has been established, ongoing multi-country studies are conducting feasibility and implementation research. The results of these studies may provide guidance on the use of available tools and monitoring the impact of such interventions. The Leprosy Research Initiative (LRI), launched at the International Leprosy Congress in 2013, aims to promote, fund, and facilitate high-quality leprosy research. It also seeks to strengthen research capacity in endemic countries and translate research findings into policy and practice. The LRI has identified five research priorities: early detection of leprosy; prevention, early detection, and effective treatment of nerve function impairment (NFI) and reactions; social inclusion of persons affected by leprosy; prevention of disability and integration of disability prevention activities into national programs and wound/limb care programs; and development of methods and tools to interrupt leprosy transmission and incidence, including expanding coverage of effective contact management and chemoprophylaxis. Over 20 projects have been supported with funding totaling approximately €5 million. At the global and regional levels, proposed actions include increasing resources for research through diversified funding sources, coordinating leprosy research via a global platform for information dissemination, identifying global and regional research centers to translate priorities into actionable studies, and analyzing research results to incorporate new technologies and strategies into services. At the national level, actions include establishing national research priorities, planning and implementing capacity-building activities to increase human resources for leprosy health research, and linking with regional and global centers to conduct studies. Effective surveillance and health information systems are critical for leprosy control. High-quality data is essential for assessing disease epidemiology and planning targeted activities. An ideal health information system should be case-based, allow reporting by all service providers (including private providers), and enable data analysis by geographical area, sex, age, and other factors. It should also facilitate drug management, contact screening, and recording of leprosy-related disabilities. Data entry should occur at levels with sufficient capacity and resources, and data quality systems should be in place to minimize errors and inform policymakers effectively. Globally, strengthening surveillance and response monitoring systems is essential. This includes engaging regional offices to facilitate data collection, supporting the development or adaptation of interoperable health information systems, and promoting integrated systems for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) and communicable diseases. Monitoring efforts should include training monitors and supporting countries' evaluation activities. Community awareness of leprosy is vital to improve understanding of the disease, encourage self-referral, and foster positive attitudes toward affected individuals. Awareness campaigns should deliver objective, positive, and culturally sensitive messages tailored to specific populations. Core messages should emphasize that leprosy is curable, treatment is free, early detection prevents disability, and there is no need to fear or stigmatize the disease. Early case detection through active case-finding and contact management is crucial. Active case-finding is recommended in high-burden or hard-to-reach areas and among high-risk groups. Retrospective screening of contacts of registered cases may also help detect leprosy early. Integrated screening campaigns for NTDs and tuberculosis (TB) may enhance public health impact and cost-effectiveness. Barriers to case detection, such as lack of awareness, fear, stigma, cultural disadvantages, physical barriers, and security issues, must be addressed. Public information campaigns, advocacy for supportive legislation, and flexible diagnostic and treatment arrangements can help overcome these challenges. In high-burden settings, active screening should target areas with higher disease rates, hard-to-reach populations, and specific groups like schoolchildren and contacts of leprosy cases. Training healthcare workers and ensuring privacy during examinations are also essential. In low-burden settings, active screening should focus on contacts and underserved communities. Integrated activities for NTDs and TB may be organized depending on available resources. Supervision of leprosy components in integrated activities should occur at least annually. Countries like Brazil and the Democratic Republic of the Congo have implemented strategies to enhance early detection, treatment, and surveillance of leprosy. These include national campaigns targeting schoolchildren, active case-finding in endemic areas, and health education to reduce stigma. Financial support from governments and international organizations has been critical in these efforts.
